classification.difficultyReason: Requires changing both functions to a common logarithmic base, solving for the intersection and integrating that result with each graph's intercepts and common vertical asymptote.

content.prompt: Sketch the following pairs of graphs on the same set of axes. Locate the point of intersection.

answer.short:
Intersection $(1,1)$.

Use change of base; both graphs have domain $x>0$ and vertical asymptote $x=0$.
answer.worked:
For $x>0$, use change of base:
$$\begin{align*}\log_4(4x)&=\log_2(2x)\\\frac{\log_2(4x)}{2}&=\log_2(2x)\\2+\log_2x&=2+2\log_2x\\\log_2x&=0\\x&=1\\y&=1\end{align*}$$
Both curves increase and have vertical asymptote $x=0$. Their $x$-intercepts are $(\tfrac14,0)$ and $(\tfrac12,0)$ respectively; neither has a $y$-intercept.

spec.description: Two logarithmic graphs on shared axes, with exact intercepts, intersection and matched curve labels.

answer.short:
Intersection $(\tfrac18,-1)$.

Use change of base; both graphs have domain $x>0$ and vertical asymptote $x=0$.
answer.worked:
For $x>0$, use change of base:
$$\begin{align*}\log_2(4x)&=\log_4(2x)\\\log_2(4x)&=\frac{\log_2(2x)}{2}\\4+2\log_2x&=1+\log_2x\\\log_2x&=-3\\x&=\frac18\\y&=\log_2\left(4\times\frac18\right)\\y&=-1\end{align*}$$
Both curves increase and have vertical asymptote $x=0$. Their $x$-intercepts are $(\tfrac14,0)$ and $(\tfrac12,0)$ respectively; neither has a $y$-intercept.
